data.content_ref: inline:{"analogy":null,"claim":"The preference for better-corroborated theories is defensible on Popper's terms as a non-inductive 'critical preference' based on verisimilitude (truth-likeness), but accepting this defense costs the admission that we can never know if our preference is actually tracking truth, only that it is the most rational guess available in the absence of induction.","counterconditions":[{"case":"The Tich\u00fd/Miller proof demonstrates that verisimilitude cannot be formally defined or compared in rich languages, potentially collapsing the distinction between 'better-corroborated' and 'more probable'.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"If acting on a theory implies expecting it to work in the future, this smuggles in an inductive assumption about the uniformity of nature.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"},{"case":"Popper's rejection of probability as a measure of corroboration must remain consistent even when practical action demands a probabilistic-looking choice.","checker_spec":null,"eval":"observation"}],"definitions":[],"derivation":[],"formalization_refs":[],"mechanism":"The mechanism distinguishes between 'justification' (which requires induction and is impossible) and 'preferability' (which relies on the logical content of tests survived). A theory that survives severe tests has higher verisimilitude potential because it has ruled out more false possibilities without being falsified itself. The preference is not a prediction of future success (induction) but a recognition of current explanatory power and informational content. We act on the best-tested theory not because it is probable, but because it is the most informative error-elimination candidate we possess.","premises":[],"schema":"deepreason-reasoning-envelope-v1","scope":{"covers":[],"excludes":[]},"simulation_refs":[],"uncertainties":[]}
